It had been a hard year with little work, and Tom had trained poorly, with no partner to spar with and never enough to eat. <break time="0.8s" /> The Gayety Club secretary had already advanced him three pounds, the losers share of the purse, and he would not lend a single penny more. <break time="0.8s" /> Tom was forty now, and he knew better than anyone how much harder it was to get into condition at forty than in youth. <break time="0.8s" /> When he stood up to leave, Lizzie kissed him, which she seldom did, and said in a low voice, You must beat him, Tom. <break time="0.8s" /> If he won, he would receive thirty pounds, enough to pay all his debts, but if he lost, he would get nothing, not even tram fare home. <break time="0.8s" /> It was two miles to the Gayety, and as he walked, he remembered the days when he had ridden to his fights in cabs with rich friends. <break time="0.8s" /> In those days he had been the heavyweight champion of New South Wales, and the men he had beaten were older and already worn out. <break time="0.8s" /> He remembered old Stowsher Bill, who had cried in the dressing room after losing to him, and only now did Tom begin to understand why.
